title: Task 1: graphs and tables
summary: After this unit you can write a band 9 overview, group and compare features, and describe data with precise, accurate language.

lessons.title: The overview and accurate data language

items.title: What Task 1 is really testing
body: Task 1 asks you to *summarise* a visual by **selecting and reporting the main features** and making comparisons where relevant. It is not a description of every number, and it is not an essay: no opinions, no causes, no predictions beyond what the chart shows.

An overview is needed from band 6 up, and band 7 needs a clear one; what lifts a script from 7 to 9 is selecting every key feature, with accurate figures and comparisons, and nothing trivial or wrong.
Aim for about 170-230 words in about 20 minutes. Longer answers rarely score higher; they usually contain more slips and more trivial detail.
list: Introduction: one sentence paraphrasing what the visual shows (what, where, when, units).
Overview: two sentences on the big picture, no figures.
Body paragraph 1: one group of features, with selected data.
Body paragraph 2: the other group, with selected data and comparisons.
items.tip: Write the overview straight after the introduction. If you run out of time, a missing conclusion costs nothing; a missing overview caps Task Achievement at band 5.

items.title: Writing the overview
body: Ask two questions before writing: *What is the overall direction?* (up, down, stable, converging) and *What stands out?* (the largest category, a reversal, an exception). The answers are your overview.
Keep it general. Figures belong in the body paragraphs. A band 9 overview is often only two sentences, but every word in it is a genuine summary of the whole visual.

examples.text: Overall, car use remained by far the most common way of commuting, although its share fell steadily, while cycling grew from a marginal option into the second most popular mode.
examples.note: Direction plus the striking change. No numbers.

examples.text: In general, the museums that attracted the most visitors in 2012 were not necessarily those that grew fastest over the decade.
examples.note: An overview for a table: a relationship, not a list.
Weak: this is a detail with figures, not an overview.

items.title: Selecting and grouping
body: With four or more categories you cannot describe each line separately and still compare. Group features that behave alike: *the two categories that rose*, *the three that declined*, *the largest and the smallest*.

Choose the paragraph split that makes comparison easy. For a line graph, it is often 'rising categories' versus 'falling categories'; for a table, it can be 'the largest values' versus 'the rest', or one year versus the other.
Every number you quote should support a comparison. 'Rail rose from 8% to 13%' is fine; listing 1990, 1995, 2000 and 2005 values for every line is not.

items.title: Precise data language
body: Band 9 lexis is precise rather than showy. Choose verbs and nouns that match the size and shape of the change, and vary the grammar: verb + adverb (*rose sharply*), adjective + noun (*a sharp rise*), and phrases such as *accounted for*, *a threefold increase*, *respectively*.
list: **rose sharply / climbed steeply**: a large, fast increase
**edged up / crept up**: a very small increase
**plateaued / levelled off**: stopped changing after a rise or fall
**fluctuated around**: went up and down without a clear trend
**accounted for / made up**: a share of a total (*cars accounted for 62% of journeys*)
**a threefold increase / tripled**: multiplied by three
**respectively**: matches two lists in order (*41% and 24% respectively*)
**peaked at / reached a high of**: the highest point
**bottomed out at / reached a low of**: the lowest point

examples.text: The share of commuters who cycled tripled between 2000 and 2015.
By 2020, cars and bicycles accounted for 41% and 24% of journeys respectively.

items.title: Approximations and accuracy
body: Real charts rarely give exact values, so use controlled approximation: *just under a quarter*, *roughly two thirds*, *almost double*, *a little over 400,000*. Do not invent precision the chart does not show.
Never explain why something happened (*because petrol became expensive*) and never judge (*a worrying fall*). These are the two most common ways strong writers lose Task Achievement in Task 1.

examples.text: just over 60% (= 62%), roughly a fifth (= 19-21%), nearly half (= 47-49%)
The number of visitors almost doubled, from 230,000 to around 440,000.

items.tip: Fractions and percentages are both fine. Mix them for flexibility, but never at the cost of accuracy: 41% is 'just over two fifths', not 'nearly half'.

items.q: A line graph shows the percentage of commuters in a city using four modes of transport, 1990-2020. Car use falls from 62% to 41%; cycling rises from 4% to 24%; bus use falls from 20% to 12%; rail rises from 8% to 11%. Which is the best overview?
options: Overall, car use fell from 62% to 41% while cycling rose from 4% to 24%.
Overall, the car remained the dominant mode of commuting despite a steady decline, while cycling saw the most dramatic growth, overtaking the bus to become the second most common choice.
Overall, it is clear that the city's policies to encourage cycling were successful.
Overall, there were many changes in how people travelled to work over the thirty years.
items.why: Option B summarises direction and the most striking feature with no figures. A is detail with numbers, C gives a cause and an opinion, and D is too vague to summarise anything.

items.q: Which sentence describes the change from 230,000 to 440,000 most accurately?
options: The figure doubled.
The figure almost doubled.
The figure rose threefold.
The figure increased slightly.
items.why: Double 230,000 would be 460,000, so 440,000 is *almost* double. 'Doubled' overstates it, and 'slightly' badly understates a 91% rise.

items.text: After rising steadily for a decade, the share of rail journeys ___ at around 13% between 2015 and 2018.
items.why: Several verbs work here: *plateaued*, *levelled off* (or *out*), *stabilised*, *held steady*, *remained* or *stayed*. Each describes a line that stops rising and stays roughly flat; *plateaued* and *levelled off* are the most precise.

items.text: In 2020, cars and bicycles accounted for 41% and 24% of all commuting journeys ___.
items.why: *Respectively* links the two figures to the two categories in the order given.

items.text: Between 2000 and 2020, cycling saw a nearly fivefold ___, from 5% to 24% of journeys.
items.why: *A fivefold increase / rise*: the noun follows the adjective *fivefold*. 5% to 24% is just under five times.

items.text: The proportion of commuters taking the bus fell from a fifth in 1990 to ___ under an eighth by 2020.
items.why: One eighth is 12.5%, so 12% is *just under* an eighth. Approximations must point in the right direction.

items.q: Each sentence describes a chart in which: cars 62% to 41%, bicycles 4% to 24%, buses 20% to 12%, rail 8% to 11% (1990 to 2020). Decide what is wrong with each one.
options: A  Accurate
B  Inaccurate comparison or figure
C  Gives a cause, opinion or prediction

rows.label: Rail was the least popular mode throughout the period.
Cycling overtook the bus as the second most common mode by 2020.
Thanks to new cycle lanes, cycling grew sixfold.
Car use declined by roughly a third over the period.
Bus use is likely to keep falling in the next decade.

items.why: Rail (8%) was more popular than cycling (4%) in 1990, so it was not always the least popular. A fall from 62% to 41% is about a third, not half. Causes ('thanks to new cycle lanes') and predictions ('likely to keep falling') are not in the chart.

items.q: Put the parts of this Task 1 response in the correct order.
items: The graph illustrates how the proportion of commuters using four modes of transport in a British city changed between 1990 and 2020.
Overall, the car remained the most common choice despite a steady decline, whereas cycling grew from a marginal option into the second most popular.
Car use stood at just over 60% in 1990 and fell gradually to 41% by the end of the period, while the share of bus passengers fell by two fifths, from a fifth to 12%.
In contrast, cycling, which accounted for only 4% of journeys in 1990, climbed steeply after 2000 to reach almost a quarter in 2020.
items.why: Introduction (paraphrase), overview (no figures), then two body paragraphs grouping declining modes and the rising mode. 'In contrast' signals the second group.

items.q: Which sentence would an examiner consider the most natural and precise?
options: The percentage of car users experienced a dramatic plummet to 41%.
The percentage of commuters who drove fell steadily to 41%.
The car users' percentage went down very much to 41%.
The percentage of car was decreased to 41%.
items.why: B is precise and accurate ('steadily' matches a gradual fall). A is inflated ('a dramatic plummet' is redundant and exaggerated), C is vague, and D has errors (*of car*, passive *was decreased*).

items.q: A table shows that Museum X had 520,000 visitors in 2012 and 860,000 in 2022. Which comparison is accurate?
options: Visitor numbers rose by roughly two thirds.
Visitor numbers almost doubled.
Visitor numbers rose by 860,000.
Visitor numbers rose by about a third.
items.why: The rise is 340,000, which is about 65% of 520,000, so 'roughly two thirds' is right. 'Almost doubled' would need about 1,000,000.

items.title: Planning a line graph in four minutes
body: Spend the first three or four minutes looking, not writing. Find the highest and lowest lines at the start and at the end, any line that crosses another, and any point where a trend changes direction.
Then decide your grouping. With four lines, a common band 9 split is 'the categories that fell' and 'the categories that rose', with crossings mentioned where they happen.
list: Introduction: paraphrase the title (what, where, when, unit).
Overview: the dominant category and the most dramatic change.
Body 1: the falling lines, with start and end figures and the shape of the fall.
Body 2: the rising lines, including the crossing point.
items.tip: Check the units. 'Percentage of commuters' is not 'number of commuters': write *the share / proportion of commuters*, never *the number of cars*.

items.prompt:
The graph below shows the percentage of commuters using four different modes of transport to travel to work in a British city between 1990 and 2020.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

visual.title: Percentage of commuters by mode of transport in a British city, 1990-2020

plan: Paraphrase: share of commuters, four modes, British city, 1990-2020.
Overview: car still dominant but falling; cycling the big riser, overtakes bus.
Body 1: car (62, peak 64, down to 41) and bus (20 to 12).
Body 2: bicycle (4, flat, then steep rise to 24) and rail (8, peak 13, 11).

text: The line graph illustrates how the share of commuters in a British city who travelled to work by car, bus, bicycle and train changed over the thirty years from 1990.

Overall, the car remained by far the most common means of getting to work, although its dominance was eroded after the mid-1990s. The most striking development was the growth of cycling, which rose from a marginal option to the second most popular mode, overtaking the bus in the process.

In 1990, just over three fifths of commuters drove to work, a figure that edged up to 64% in 1995 before falling continuously to 41% by 2020, a decline of roughly a third. Bus use also declined, though by fewer percentage points: having accounted for a fifth of journeys at the start of the period, it fell to 15% by 2000 and then drifted down to 12%.

Cycling, by contrast, was the least common mode in 1990, at only 4%, and changed little for a decade. After 2000, however, it climbed steeply, overtaking rail around 2010 and the bus shortly afterwards, and by 2020 almost a quarter of commuters cycled, a sixfold increase on the original figure. Rail use grew gradually from 8% to a peak of 13% in 2015, before slipping back to 11% in the final five years.
notes: The overview identifies the two key features (car dominance in decline, the rise of cycling) without any figures.
Grouping by direction (falling modes, then rising modes) makes comparison natural and avoids a line-by-line list.
Data language is precise and varied: *edged up*, *drifted down*, *climbed steeply*, *a sixfold increase*, *slipping back*.
Approximations are accurate: 62% is 'just over three fifths', 62% to 41% is 'roughly a third' lower.
No causes or opinions are given, even though the trend invites speculation about cycle lanes or fuel prices.
Cohesion comes from structure and reference (*a figure that*, *in the process*, *by contrast*) rather than a string of linkers.

items.title: Tables: find the story before you write
body: A table gives you numbers without a shape, so the danger is listing them row by row. Before writing, rank the rows, calculate the rough size of each change, and look for a relationship between columns.

In this task, look at how the last column relates to growth. You must not say *why* (that would be speculation), but you can report the pattern: *all three museums that grew drew a larger share of their visitors from overseas (26-41%) than the two that shrank (8-12%)*.
list: Rank: which was largest in 2012 and in 2022? Did the ranking change?
Direction: which rose, which fell?
Size: roughly how much (by a third, almost doubled, fell by a third)?
Third column: how does it relate to the others?
items.tip: Round sensibly: '860' in a column headed 'thousands' is 860,000 visitors. Write the unit in full at least once.

items.prompt:
The table below shows the number of visitors to five museums in a European city in 2012 and 2022, and the percentage of visitors in 2022 who came from overseas.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

visual.title: Visitors to five museums in a European city, 2012 and 2022
head: Museum
Visitors 2012 (thousands)
Visitors 2022 (thousands)
Overseas visitors 2022 (%)

plan: Paraphrase: visitors to five museums, 2012 and 2022, plus share from overseas.
Overview: three grew, Modern Art fastest and now top; the growers all have higher overseas shares.
Body 1: the growers (Natural History, Modern Art, City History) with sizes of change.
Body 2: the decliners (Maritime, Toy) plus the overseas column compared.

text: The table compares annual visitor numbers at five museums in a European city in 2012 and 2022, and also shows what proportion of each museum's visitors in 2022 came from abroad.

Overall, three of the five museums attracted more visitors over the decade, with the Museum of Modern Art growing far faster than any other and overtaking the Natural History Museum as the most visited. There is also a clear pattern in the final column: all three museums that grew drew a larger share of their visitors from overseas than the two that declined.

In 2012, the Natural History Museum was the most popular, with 690,000 visitors, followed by the Museum of Modern Art at 520,000. Ten years later, the latter had risen by about two thirds to 860,000, while the former grew only slightly, to 720,000. The City History Museum also expanded considerably, from 230,000 to 310,000, an increase of around a third.

The remaining two museums lost visitors. Attendance at the Maritime Museum dipped from 410,000 to 380,000, and the Toy and Childhood Museum, already the smallest, saw its figure fall by roughly a third to 95,000. As for overseas visitors, they made up 41% of the total at the Museum of Modern Art, 35% at the Natural History Museum and just over a quarter at the City History Museum, compared with 12% at the Maritime Museum and only 8% at the Toy and Childhood Museum.
notes: The overview reports both the main change (the ranking reversal at the top) and the relationship between columns, without figures.
Paragraphs group museums by direction (growth versus decline) instead of going row by row.
Changes are expressed as proportions (*about two thirds*, *around a third*) as well as raw figures, which shows real analysis of the data.
Reference (*the latter*, *the former*, *the remaining two museums*) keeps the text cohesive without heavy linkers.
The writer notes the pattern in overseas visitors but does not speculate about why it exists, which keeps the response within Task 1.

items.title: Bar charts: grouping and ranking
body: A bar chart with five categories and two years invites a list: this one rose, that one fell. Resist it. First rank the categories in each year, then group those that moved the same way, so that each paragraph compares a group rather than walking through the bars one by one.

Ranking language lets you compare without quoting every figure: superlatives for the extremes, multiples for large gaps, and small-difference phrases for near ties. Check each phrase against the bars: *twice as many* must really be about double, and *slightly ahead of* suits a gap of a point or two, not ten.
list: **the most / the least common**: *cash was the most common method in 2014*
**the second most popular / ranked third**
**by far the largest / a close second**
**twice / three times as many as**: *more than twice as many contactless payments as mobile ones*
**slightly ahead of / just behind / almost level with**: for a gap of a point or two
**overtook / was overtaken by**: when the order changes between the two years
**accounted for / made up**: a share of all payments
items.tip: With two years and five categories, the strongest split is usually 'what shrank' and 'what grew'. Mention a small, stable category in one clause: examiners reward selection, not completeness.

items.q: In 2024, contactless cards accounted for 46% of payments and mobile phones for 21%. Which comparison is accurate?
options: Contactless payments were three times as common as payments by mobile phone.
Contactless payments were more than twice as common as payments by mobile phone.
Contactless payments were slightly ahead of payments by mobile phone.
Payments by mobile phone were almost as common as contactless ones.
items.why: Twice 21% is 42%, so 46% is *more than twice* as common. *Three times* would need about 63%, and *slightly ahead of* suits a gap of a point or two, not 25.

items.q: In 2024, chip-and-PIN cards accounted for 15% of payments and cash for 14%. Which sentence fits best?
options: Chip and PIN was slightly ahead of cash.
Chip and PIN was far more popular than cash.
Cash overtook chip and PIN.
Chip and PIN was twice as common as cash.
items.why: One percentage point is a near tie, so *slightly ahead of* (or *just ahead of*) is exact. Cash did not overtake chip and PIN: in 2024 it was just behind it.

items.prompt:
The bar chart below shows the methods people used to pay for purchases in shops in one European country in 2014 and 2024.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

visual.title: Methods of payment in shops in one European country, 2014 and 2024 (% of all payments)

plan: Paraphrase: how shoppers paid, five methods, one European country, 2014 and 2024.
Overview: a shift from cash and inserted cards to contactless and mobile; contactless became by far the most common.
Body 1: the two methods that shrank (cash, chip and PIN), including the change in order between them.
Body 2: the two that grew (contactless, mobile), compared with each other; 'other' in one clause.

text: The bar chart compares the proportion of shop purchases in one European country that were paid for in cash, by chip-and-PIN card, by contactless card, by mobile phone or by other means in 2014 and 2024.

Overall, the decade saw a decisive shift away from cash and inserted cards towards contactless methods. Contactless cards, a marginal option at the start of the period, had become by far the most common way to pay ten years later, while notes and coins lost their place as the leading method.

In 2014, just over half of all payments were made in cash and a further third by chip and PIN, so these two methods together accounted for 85% of transactions. By 2024, the share of cash had collapsed to 14%, little more than a quarter of its earlier level, and chip-and-PIN payments had more than halved to 15%, leaving the two almost level, with the card now slightly ahead.

The newer methods moved in the opposite direction. Contactless payments rose from only 6% to 46%, almost an eightfold increase, and the share made by mobile phone climbed from a negligible 1% to just over a fifth. Even so, contactless payments remained more than twice as common as mobile ones. The remaining category, other methods, was minor throughout, and its share halved from 8% to 4%.
notes: The overview gives the overall shift and the change at the top of the ranking without a single figure.
The body paragraphs group the methods by direction: the two older methods that shrank, then the two newer ones that grew, with *other* in a single clause because it is minor.
Ranking and comparison language does the analysis: *by far the most common*, *almost level*, *slightly ahead*, *more than twice as common*.
Derived figures are checked against the bars: 52% + 33% = 85%; 14% is a little more than a quarter of 52%; 6% to 46% is almost eightfold; 21% is just over a fifth.
Nothing is invented or explained: the chart gives no reasons, so the answer gives none.

lessons.title: Timed Task 1: pie charts and a table

items.prompt:
You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.

The pie charts below show how the household waste collected in a British city was dealt with in 2005 and 2025. The table shows the amount of household waste produced per person in the same two years.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

visual.title: How household waste was dealt with in a British city, 2005 and 2025 (%)

visual2.title: Household waste produced per person in the same city (kg per year)
head: Type of waste

plan: Paraphrase both visuals: what happened to household waste (pies) and how much each person produced (table), 2005 and 2025.
Overview: landfill replaced by recycling, composting and energy; less waste per person, except plastics.
Body 1: the pies, led by the biggest changes (landfill, recycling), then energy and composting.
Body 2: the table: the total, the two largest falls, and plastics as the exception.

text: The pie charts show how a British city dealt with its household waste in 2005 and 2025, and the table gives the amount produced per person, by type, in the same years.

Overall, the city moved decisively away from landfill, and by 2025 most of its rubbish was recycled, composted or burnt to produce energy. At the same time, each resident was throwing away considerably less, although plastics went against this trend.

In 2005, just over three fifths of household waste went to landfill, with recycling a distant second at 18% and incineration for energy at 12%. By 2025, the landfill share had fallen to under a tenth. Recycling had more than doubled to 41%, making it the main method, energy recovery had grown to almost a third, and the proportion composted had nearly tripled, from 6% to 17%. Other methods accounted for 2% in both years.

According to the table, the total produced per person fell by about a fifth, from 520 to 410 kilograms a year. Paper and card declined most steeply in relative terms, by over two fifths to 70 kg, while food and garden waste, the largest category in both years, dropped by the same absolute amount, 50 kg, to 140. The other two categories also decreased, but more modestly. Plastics were the only exception, rising by a third to 60 kg.
notes: Two visuals, one overview: the sentence on landfill sums up the pie charts and the sentence on waste per person sums up the table, with no figures in either.
The pies are compared by what changed most (landfill and recycling) and by rank, not slice by slice in the order of the key.
Approximations are checked: 62% is *just over three fifths*, 9% *under a tenth*, 31% *almost a third*, 6% to 17% *nearly tripled*.
The table paragraph separates relative from absolute change: paper and card fell further in proportion, but by the same 50 kilograms as food and garden waste.
The exception, plastics, is singled out: selecting the feature that breaks the pattern is what examiners reward.
No causes are offered, although recycling schemes or packaging habits would be tempting explanations.
